notes.meaning: Rehoboam was Solomon's son and the rightful heir to David's throne. The northern tribes gathered at Shechem, an old meeting place in the land of Ephraim, instead of coming to Jerusalem. Commentators see this choice as a warning sign that the tribes were already leaning toward breaking away.

Jeroboam had fled to Egypt after the prophet Ahijah told him he would one day rule ten tribes (1 Kings 11). Now Solomon was dead, and the news reached him. Matthew Henry says Jeroboam knew what God had planned for him and was waiting for the promised crown.

The tribes sent for Jeroboam, and he spoke for them. They asked Rehoboam to lighten the "yoke," meaning the heavy taxes and forced work of Solomon's reign. They promised to serve him if he did. Matthew Henry notes they said nothing about Solomon's worship of other gods; they cared only about money and labor.
Rehoboam asked for three days to think it over. Taking time to weigh the request calmly was wise in itself. But Matthew Henry notes the delay also gave unhappy people time to plan their revolt.
Rehoboam first turned to the older men who had advised Solomon. Asking them was a sensible step. They had years of experience at his father's side.

The elders' advice was simple. Serve the people today and speak kindly to them, and they will serve you for life. Commentators draw a lasting lesson: the way to lead is to serve. Adam Clarke says a good king lives for his people, not for himself.

Rehoboam turned down the elders and went to the young men he had grown up with. They were about his own age but had little experience. Matthew Henry warns that pleasant friends are not always good advisers.

Rehoboam repeated the people's request to the young men and asked how to answer. He had already rejected the elders before he asked, so he seems to have been looking for advisers who would agree with him. The Geneva Notes say nothing is harder for people in power than to control their own wishes and follow good advice.

The young men gave him a boastful speech. "My little finger is thicker than my father's waist" was a saying meaning "my power is far greater than his." He would add to their burden. He would punish with "scorpions" instead of whips, likely whips set with sharp iron points that tore the flesh.
Jeroboam and the people came back on the third day, just as the king had told them. The Geneva Notes point out that the people showed respect here. They did nothing until the king gave his answer.

Rehoboam spoke harshly and used the young men's words almost exactly. Matthew Henry notes he even agreed that his father had been harsh, which was unfair to Solomon's memory. Pride and a hunger for total power blinded him. One writer says a dozen rash words opened the door to centuries of trouble.

The writer says this turn of events was from the LORD. It kept the promise God gave Jeroboam through Ahijah, and it was a punishment for Solomon's worship of idols. God left Rehoboam to his own foolishness and used it to carry out His plan. God works out His purposes even through people's mistakes and sins.

differ.view: God gave Rehoboam over to his own mistake and hid from him what would have brought peace. God also arranged events so the kingdom would be torn from him.
God had no part in Rehoboam's sin, yet He was mysteriously at work in it all, much as at the cross. People act freely, and God still rules.
Methodist teachers are split. Some say God gave Rehoboam up to his mistake. Others say the cause was Rehoboam's own folly and cruelty, and only the tribes' turning away came from the LORD.

notes.meaning: The northern tribes answered with an old battle cry. "What portion do we have in David?" meant they wanted nothing more to do with David's family. "To your tents" meant "go home; he is not our king." Matthew Henry notes how quickly they forgot all the good David had done, and the Geneva Notes call their words rash, even though their complaint was fair.

Rehoboam still ruled the Israelites who lived in Judah's towns. Here begins a lasting split: "Israel" in the north and Judah in the south. Matthew Henry counts it to Judah's credit that they stayed loyal to David's family.

Rehoboam sent Adoram, the man in charge of forced labor, who is also called Adoniram. He was the very man the people hated most, so sending him was another foolish move. The crowd stoned him to death, and Rehoboam fled in his chariot to Jerusalem.

From then on, the northern tribes stayed apart from David's royal family. The Geneva Notes see this as God's just judgment for Solomon's sins. Still, commentators say that turning against the family God had chosen to rule was itself a serious sin.

When the northern tribes heard Jeroboam was back, they made him king. Only Judah stayed with David's family, along with Benjamin, which was closely tied to it. Keil and Delitzsch say taking the throne this way was Jeroboam's first sin, even though God had promised him the kingdom. Adam Clarke says only God's just judgment explains it.

Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam gathered 180,000 soldiers from Judah and Benjamin to win back the north by force. The Geneva Notes say he still did not see that the LORD had planned this split. Matthew Henry sees it as a natural wish to recover what he had lost.

God sent Shemaiah with a clear message. ("Man of God" means a prophet.) Do not fight your brothers; go home, "for this word is from Me." The split was God's doing and was not to be undone, and Rehoboam and the people obeyed. Matthew Henry draws the lesson that when we know God's will, we should accept it even when it goes against what we want.
Jeroboam strengthened and fortified Shechem and made it his first capital. He also rebuilt Penuel, east of the Jordan River. It guarded an important trade road and his eastern border.

Jeroboam worried in private. If his people kept going to the temple in Jerusalem for the feasts, their hearts might turn back to Rehoboam, and they might kill him. God had promised him a lasting family line if he obeyed (11:38), but he did not trust that promise. Matthew Henry says that not truly believing God is enough lies at the root of all our turning away from Him.

After getting advice, Jeroboam made two golden calves, probably young bulls. He told the people the trip to Jerusalem was too much for them, and he used the same words Aaron spoke over the golden calf at Mount Sinai. Traditional commentators think he meant the calves to stand for the true God of Israel, not a foreign god. Even so, it broke God's command against worshiping Him through images and opened the door to worse idol worship.

differ.view: The plural word "gods" shows these were plainly false gods, not the LORD at all.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think Jeroboam's worship was traditional and aimed at the LORD, with the calves as stands for the unseen God, like the cherubim in Judah. They think the story was told to echo Exodus 32 and make Jeroboam look bad.

notes.meaning: He put one calf at Bethel, near the southern border with Judah, and one at Dan in the far north. Both places had old religious history. Jacob met God at Bethel, and Dan already had an image shrine from the days of the judges. This made the new worship feel familiar and convenient.

This "became a sin." It broke God's law in two ways: it worshiped Him through images, and it left the place He had chosen for His name. People traveled far, even to Dan, to worship before the calves. Matthew Henry notes that people who found Jerusalem too far were happy to go farther to worship their own way.

Jeroboam also built shrines on the "high places," which were hilltop worship sites. He made priests from any family. But God's law said priests must come from the tribe of Levi, the tribe He set apart for this work. The Levites seem to have refused to serve the calves and moved to Judah (2 Chronicles 11:13-14).

Jeroboam started his own festival in the eighth month. It copied the Feast of Tabernacles (also called Booths), which God had set for the seventh month. He may have pointed to the later harvest in the north as a reason, but commentators say the real aim was to cut the people's ties to Jerusalem while keeping something that looked familiar. He offered sacrifices at Bethel and placed his new priests there.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 32-33 were added later to strengthen the case against Jeroboam.

notes.meaning: The writer stresses that this was a month "of his own choosing," not God's. Jeroboam also offered the sacrifices himself, taking a priest's role and joining the power of the throne and the altar in one person. Matthew Henry notes that King Uzziah was later struck with leprosy for doing the same. This sets the scene for the prophet who comes to Bethel in the next chapter.
